query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In five-metal near-equiatomic nanoparticles initially crystallized as a single-phase solid solution, the presence of a stable surface passivation layer governs structural and chemical stability by reducing high-temperature surface diffusion of reactive elements. Under passivation, the nanoparticles retain their single-phase composition from 473 K up to 1923 K, whereas unpassivated samples experience surface-mediated segregation and eventual phase decomposition at elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase, near-equiatomic five-metal nanoparticles with uniform elemental distribution, prepared in a solid-solution state.
generation.intervention: Perform in situ high-temperature environmental (S)TEM with EDS and EELS on two sets of nanoparticles from 473 K to 1923 K: one set with a stable passivation layer (e.g., oxide or nitride) on the surface and one set unpassivated.
generation.conditions: Temperatures ranging from 473 K to 1923 K in mildly reactive or inert atmospheres typical of catalytic and thermoelectric environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Surface passivation layer, which can suppress selective oxidation or segregation of more reactive species.
generation.mechanism: Passivation reduces the driving force for surface diffusion by chemically stabilizing the local atomic environment, thereby minimizing growth of any composition gradients or second-phase precipitates at high temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unpassivated control, passivated nanoparticles will show minimal segregation and maintain near-equiatomic compositions and single-phase structure through the full temperature range, while unpassivated samples develop localized chemical fluctuations and multiple phases above ~1000 K, eventually degrading.
generation.baseline: Initial single-phase near-equiatomic nanoparticles before any high-temperature treatments or exposure.
generation.boundary: Applicable to five-metal nanoparticles with well-adhered passivation layers; breakdown or instability of the passivation coating at high temperature would invalidate the effect.
generation.uncertainty: Exact temperature thresholds for phase decomposition and passivation stability remain unverified, and may vary with specific compositions and processing methods.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two identical batches of near-equiatomic five-metal nanoparticles. Coat one batch with a robust passivation layer. Subject both batches to identical temperature ramps (473–1923 K) under controlled atmosphere using in situ environmental (S)TEM. Compare real-time structural evolution, elemental segregation, and phase formation between passivated versus unpassivated batches.
measurements: Electron diffraction patterns and high-resolution TEM images to identify phase formation or transformations
Elemental distribution profiles via EDS/EELS line scans and mapping
Surface morphology changes tracked with in situ imaging
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Observation of similar high-temperature phase segregation or decomposition in the passivated samples relative to unpassivated controls, or the absence of segregation in the unpassivated samples, would disprove the hypothesis.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.

decision.trend: Early work (PMC7512559, 2018-12-12) on the equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy revealed that while the single-phase FCC matrix remains largely stable at 500–600 °C, microstructural changes such as dynamic precipitation can occur under stress. Later, powder-metallurgy studies of the HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy system (PMC6926650, 2019-12-03) showed near-single-phase bcc microstructures stable at elevated temperatures, but the full response over the entire 473–1923 K range remains understudied. More recent simulation-based work (PMC11375216, 2024-09-04) demonstrated modest thermal stability benefits from chemical short-range order in bcc HfNbTaTiZr up to ~1300 K, leaving open questions on nanoparticle-scale phase stability at higher temperatures and under reactive environments. Together, these results suggest that while entropic mixing can preserve overall alloy uniformity at moderate to high temperatures, surface-mediated segregation and phase separation in nanoparticle form remain poorly understood.
decision.unsolved: It is not yet clear to what extent high-entropy stabilization alone can ensure a single-phase solid solution in five-or-more-metal nanoparticles when exposed to 473–1923 K in catalytic or thermoelectric environments. Surface energy effects, chemical potential differences, and short-range order may each drive local segregation at high temperatures or under reactive gases. A direct, real-time understanding of elemental redistribution and phase transformations during heating is needed to resolve this open question.
decision.lever: Perform in situ high-temperature environmental (scanning) transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) and electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) mapping on single-phase, five-metal nanoparticles heated from 473 K to 1923 K in controlled atmospheres, comparing surface-passivated vs. non-passivated samples.
decision.why: Building on observations of partial phase stability in bulk high-entropy alloys and the known sensitivity of nanoparticles to high-temperature environments, direct in situ characterization is the logical next step. By monitoring structural and compositional changes in real time over the wide operating range, one can test whether the energetic benefit of multicomponent mixing fully prevents phase separation or segregation. This extends the temperature range and cat/thermoelectric conditions that have been only partially explored, thus providing a definitive test of nanostructural stability.
